paras: The averted lynching at Victoria, Mississippi, took place on January 20, 1903, when a crowd of about 500 people gathered as two Black men suspected of murdering Oneal Jones were brought to Victoria for a preliminary hearing. No attack was made, and the prisoners were returned to jail at Holly Springs; a dispatch carried under the headline "Lynching Averted" said that a lynching had been expected.

The two men, whose names the report does not give, were held in the Holly Springs jail as the "suspected murderers" of Oneal Jones. Victoria lay near the scene of the killing, and the men were taken there for a preliminary trial before Justice Benson.

When the prisoners arrived in Victoria on the morning of January 20, about 500 people had assembled. According to the Holly Springs dispatch, a lynching "would probably have occurred had a trial taken place and guilt fixed upon them." The two men instead waived examination, which ended the hearing without testimony.

Judge Lowrey and District Attorney Roane attended to use their influence for peace if needed, and several ministers were present as "pacificators." The prisoners were then brought back to Holly Springs and lodged in jail.
The men were remanded to jail to await the circuit court term in February. No report of their trial or of any action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The only report found was the Holly Springs dispatch printed on the front page of the Times-Promoter on January 23, 1903. Its headlines, "Lynching Averted" and "Suspected Murderers of Oneal Jones Escape the Noose," framed the day around the prisoners' escape from the crowd. The dispatch called the men "negroes" and "suspected murderers," and it treated a lynching as the likely result of a finding of guilt without comment on the crowd. No account in the Black press was found.
